question: A 60-year-old man describes central chest tightness radiating to the left jaw, onset at rest, lasting 20 minutes, with associated diaphoresis. Which feature MOST strongly suggests an ischaemic rather than musculoskeletal aetiology?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Quality helps (pressure/tightness is typical of ischaemia) but is not the single strongest discriminator.

answers.text: Radiation to the left jaw with diaphoresis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Radiation to the jaw or left arm combined with autonomic features (diaphoresis, nausea) is highly specific for ischaemia. Musculoskeletal pain does not radiate in this pattern and is not associated with diaphoresis.
Duration distinguishes stable angina (<15 min, resolves with GTN) from UA/NSTEMI (>20 min), but alone does not differentiate ischaemia from other causes.
Rest onset is characteristic of UA/NSTEMI but also occurs in oesophageal spasm and aortic dissection.

overallFeedback.feedback: The combination of radiation to jaw/left arm WITH diaphoresis is the most specific cluster for ischaemia. Any one feature alone is less discriminating.
Excellent. Jaw/left arm radiation plus autonomic features is a high-specificity cluster for ACS requiring immediate ECG.
